cue: Hold still and watch. A jumping spider sees a small sharp strip well, and the rest of the scene in movement.

cpd.note: principal eye acuity of Portia fimbriata; the family's other species are lower

fov.note: whole-animal field from the secondary eyes, near 300 to 360 degrees

fovea.note: scale of the sharp middle; chosen by the app from the narrow principal-eye field

gate.note: how much still things fade; movement is favoured but still objects stay faint

sat.note: colour is kept, as the principal eyes see colour

fall.note: how fast sharpness falls with light

topoA.note: sharpness falls from the middle along the long axis, by analogy with other small predators

uvBlue.note: the blue channel stands in for ultraviolet

JUMP.note: a dichromat's view: ultraviolet and green receptors, the blue channel standing in for ultraviolet

rows: The principal eyes resolve fine detail better than most animals of this size. A Portia spider reaches about 12 cycles per degree, and a Phidippus about 4, so the sharpest part of the picture is near a person's own.

The principal eyes see only a thin upright strip, about 2 degrees wide and 21 high in Phidippus johnsoni. The spider turns its eyes to scan across the scene, so the sharp strip moves over the picture.
Four pairs of eyes see the rest of the world. The side eyes see movement across nearly the whole circle around the spider, and they are much blurrier.

Jumping spiders have two colour receptors in the principal eyes, one ultraviolet and one green. Saitis barbipes and Plexippus validus both showed these two classes, so the picture is a dichromat's picture.
The side eyes respond to movement and little else, and a still object stays unseen until it moves. Metaphidippus harfordi turned only to targets that moved.
Sharpness falls away from the middle, the blue channel stands in for ultraviolet, and the glow and the lingering picture are the app's drawing. None of these numbers is measured in this animal.
Some settings in this view are the app's own choices, because no measurement gives them. They are set to give a fair picture of the animal and can be tuned by hand.

field.name: wedge
field.note: the sharp strip shown as a wedge
